newsitem.title: UK: Sterling ratchets up to new highs against mark.
newsitem.headline: Sterling ratchets up to new highs against mark.

text.p: Sterling leapt to its highest levels in more than six-and-a-half years against the mark amid broad-based weakness in the German currency and persistent expectations of higher UK interest rates.

"The mark is collapsing and numbers like 3.10 (per pound) are looking reasonable for the end of the year," said Peter von Maydell, currency economist at UBS. "Last week sterling was ramping up on its own but now its gains are more dollar led."
Sterling/mark rose as high as 3.0243, the strongest it has been since October 1990. It was at 3.0235/42 at 0945 GMT from 2.9985/95 late Friday in Europe.
The pound's rise came as the dollar ratcheted up to 1.7960 marks, its best showing since August 1991 and the mark slumped to 63.60 yen, the weakest it has been in almost 23 months.
The dollar's gains prevented cable from keeping pace with sterling/mark and the pound fell to $1.6870/80 from $1.6933/43 late Friday in Europe.
Traders said there was no sign yet of UK central bank intervention to cap the pound's rise.
"The Bank of England does not seem too worried at these levels given their main concern is inflation," said a London-based trader.
Sterling has ratcheted almost five percent higher against the mark so far this month, and climbed 3.4 percent against a trade-weighted basket of 20 currencies.

These gains have been largely driven by mounting evidence of the strength of UK domestic demand which has stoked expectations of higher UK rates. Rate-rise talk intensified after the UK budget early this month which traders said did little to curb consumption.
September short sterling was last down two basis points at 92.85. This implies rates of 7.15 percent by the end of the third quarter compared with current base rates of 6.75 percent.
"There has been a lot of focus on positive fundamentals in the UK," said Steve Barrow, economist at Banque National de Paris.

Expectations UK rates will rise further in the coming months were undented by a report on Monday which showed UK producer prices fell by more than economists had expected in June. Prices of goods leaving British factory gates fell 0.2 percent in June, while the cost of raw materials dropped 0.8 percent.
The pound's strength against the currencies of Britain's main trading partners is making imported goods less expensive in sterling terms and forcing UK companies to cut prices.

Economists expect sterling optimism to be punctured eventually as the erosion in UK exporters' competitiveness causes a widening in the trade deficit. A survey by Reuters shows that economists on average expect the pound to close the year at 2.83 marks.
Sterling bulls are happy to drive the pound higher against the mark before then, though.
"We should see 3.0360 in the next couple of days," said the London-based trader.
